section_summary: This section consists chiefly of September–October 1937 clippings from Lima’s La Prensa documenting a polemic over Japanese immigration, landholding, cotton production, commerce, and alleged political influence in Peru. José Manuel Ramírez y González, Guillermo Salinas Cossío, J. D. L., and Carlos Enrique Paz Soldán warn of economic penetration or racial and political danger, while Japanese journalists Akio Banno and H. Ikeyama reject claims of racial inferiority and government-directed colonization and emphasize Japanese contributions to agriculture. Several articles examine the Chancay Valley, the cotton trade, import quotas, and Peru’s trade balance with Japan; the final letter begins a statistical argument about Japanese control of Chancay and continues beyond this section.

subfiles.title: La infiltración japonesa — Letter from José Manuel Ramírez y González
subfiles.doc_type: newspaper clipping of a letter to the editor
subfiles.about: Ramírez argues that Japanese immigration, land acquisition, and economic organization constitute a government-directed political danger to Peru and Latin America.
subfiles.summary: Ramirez distinguishes patriotism from hostility to Japanese, alleging Japanese settlers absorb land with Tokyo's organized support and linking China's events to a warning about Amazon expansion.

subfiles.title: Submission of “El Mejoramiento de la Raza y la Inmigración Asiática”
subfiles.doc_type: newspaper clipping of a letter to the editor
subfiles.about: Banno submits an article on racial improvement and Asian immigration for publication in La Prensa.
subfiles.summary: Akio Banno, director of Lima Nippo, forwards his article on racial improvement and Asian immigration for La Prensa's discussion.

subfiles.title: Refutamos el concepto de que la raza amarilla es inferior a la raza blanca
subfiles.about: Banno rejects assertions that Asian or Japanese people are racially inferior to white people.
subfiles.summary: Banno argues education, health and ability, not color, determine achievement, citing Japan's modernization as proof the Japanese are not inferior.

subfiles.title: La infiltración japonesa — Expansión, no hegemonía comercial japonesa
subfiles.about: An unsigned critic disputes Ikeyama’s distinction between Japanese commercial expansion and political hegemony and connects Japanese cotton cultivation abroad to strategic policy.
subfiles.summary: Article argues Japanese economic expansion becomes political hegemony, Peru must protect its industry, land and trade, and Japanese cotton cultivation in several countries is a coordinated supply effort.

subfiles.title: La infiltración japonesa — Letter signed J. D. L.
subfiles.doc_type: newspaper clipping of a letter to the editor
subfiles.about: The writer agrees that Japanese people are not racially inferior but argues that organized, unassimilated Japanese settlements pose an economic and political threat.
subfiles.summary: J. D. L. accepts Banno's rejection of racial inferiority but says Japan's strength increases the danger; communities stay separate and buy farmland with Tokyo's help.

subfiles.title: Nuevos puntos sobre nuevas íes
subfiles.about: Ikeyama answers Ramírez’s accusations by denying that Japanese farmers are acquiring Peruvian land under a plan directed by Tokyo.
subfiles.summary: Ikeyama says Japanese farmers in Chancay are tenants recruited by a Peruvian landowner, reads Ogishima's report as cooperation with Peruvian authorities, and denies government-controlled colonization.

subfiles.title: La penetración japonesa en el Perú
subfiles.about: Paz Soldán places Japanese immigration within a racialized public-health and eugenic discussion of population policy in Peru and the Americas.
subfiles.summary: Paz Soldan recalls his writings since 1917 on eugenic repopulation, cites Japanese hygienists as evidence of organized study of South America, and says immigration policy should consider long-term racial effects.

subfiles.title: El Comercio entre el Japón y el Perú, III
subfiles.about: Salinas analyzes Peru’s trade balance with Japan, the cotton trade, and the quota agreements limiting Japanese manufactured imports.
subfiles.summary: Salinas reviews 1929-1936 trade: Peru's surplus came mostly from cotton and restrictions on Japanese goods; he questions long-term stability and favors temporary quotas before a lasting treaty.

subfiles.title: Un punto sobre cada i: Inmigración japonesa e industrias agrícolas peruanas, II
subfiles.about: Ikeyama recounts the history of contracted Japanese agricultural labor and argues that Japanese immigrants contributed substantially to Peru’s sugar and cotton industries.
subfiles.summary: Ikeyama traces Japanese immigration from 800 contract laborers in 1899, hardship on sugar estates, a move to cotton and trades, and denies Tokyo directed settlers.

subfiles.title: Cuatro quintas partes del Valle de Chancay cultivadas por japoneses — El deber patriótico de la generación presente
subfiles.doc_type: newspaper clipping of a letter to the editor, opening portion
subfiles.about: Ramírez begins a quantitative rebuttal to Ikeyama, alleging that Japanese farmers control more than four-fifths of the Chancay Valley and exclude Peruvians from independent economic activity.
subfiles.summary: Writer states Japanese enterprises hold 7,200 of Chancay Valley's about 12,000 hectares, giving control of commerce, transport and professions; continues beyond page 231.
